Operator Capability Levels summary:

Level 1 — Basic Install
  CR applied → correct Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps created
  Example: most 'Hello World' operators

Level 2 — Seamless Upgrades
  Knows the safe upgrade path: drain, backup, apply, verify
  Example: prometheus-operator version bumps

Level 3 — Full Lifecycle
  Backup, restore, failure detection, auto-failover
  Example: Crunchy postgres-operator, Strimzi Kafka operator

Level 4 — Deep Insights
  Prometheus metrics, ServiceMonitors, pre-wired alerts
  Example: prometheus-operator, Elasticsearch operator

Level 5 — Autopilot
  Self-scales, self-tunes, self-heals without human decisions
  Example: Google's internal Spanner operator (not public)

words.etymology: Operator Capability Levels — the taxonomy was formalised by Red Hat and the Operator Framework community in 2019 as part of the OperatorHub certification programme.

words.shortDefinition: Controller client pattern using a local cache backed by List+Watch to avoid flooding the API server with direct calls.
words.simpleDefinition: The Informer pattern provides controllers with an efficient, consistent view of Kubernetes resources. Instead of calling the API server on every reconcile, an Informer opens a persistent watch connection, maintains a local in-memory cache of all objects, and pushes change events to a rate-limited work queue. Controllers read from the local cache and write only to the API server.
words.longDefinition: The Kubernetes API server exposes a watch endpoint for every resource type. A client opening GET /apis/apps/v1/deployments?watch=true receives a long-lived HTTP response streaming WatchEvent objects (type: ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED plus the full resource) as changes occur in etcd. An Informer wraps this raw watch stream with two additional layers. The in-memory cache (Store/Indexer) keeps all objects of the watched type locally with support for indexed lookups (e.g., 'all Pods on node X'). The event handlers and work queue receive ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED events and push the changed object's NamespacedName key into a rate-limited, deduplicated work queue; reconcile worker goroutines drain the queue. Informers also implement resync — periodically re-enqueuing every cached object to trigger a full reconcile and catch drifts that produce no watch event. A SharedInformerFactory ensures multiple controllers watching the same resource type share a single watch connection and cache, not N separate connections. In kube-controller-manager, all 30+ built-in controllers share informers this way. Reading from the informer cache rather than the live API server is an absolute requirement for controllers operating at scale — each additional direct API call under load degrades API server performance for all cluster components.
words.connector: Think of the Informer pattern like a local newspaper subscription: instead of calling the press office for every story, you receive the daily paper, and your team reads from the stack. New editions arrive automatically; the press office only hears from you when you place an order (write to the API).
words.techContext: Our controller reads from the informer cache for all Get calls in reconcile; the API server only sees our write traffic — roughly 1 write per reconcile instead of 3–4 reads plus a write.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from direct API calls to informer cache reads dropped our reconciler's average API server request rate by 85% and eliminated the throttling errors we were seeing at peak load.

codeExample.code:
Informer architecture:

  etcd
    ↓
  API server (watch endpoint)
    ↓
  [Reflector]           ← reconnects on disconnect; handles resource version
    ↓
  [DeltaFIFO Queue]     ← ordered change buffer
    ↓
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  [Store / Indexer]           │  ← in-memory cache; all reconcile reads happen here
  │  [Event Handlers]            │  ← OnAdd / OnUpdate / OnDelete callbacks
  └──────────────────────────────┘
              ↓
  [Rate-Limited Work Queue]      ← deduplicated; one entry per changed object key
              ↓
  [Reconcile Worker Goroutines]  ← N workers drain the queue

  Reads: cache only.  Writes: direct to API server.

words.etymology: Informer from Latin informare ('to give form to, instruct'); the Informer as a Kubernetes programming pattern was formalized in the client-go library (circa 2016) and documented in the Kubernetes controller-runtime package.

words.shortDefinition: Cluster-scoped RBAC types that grant permissions across all namespaces, unlike namespace-scoped Role and RoleBinding.
words.simpleDefinition: A ClusterRole is an RBAC permission set that governs access to cluster-wide resources (Nodes, PersistentVolumes, Namespaces, StorageClasses, CRDs) and can optionally span all namespaces. A ClusterRoleBinding attaches a ClusterRole to subjects with cluster-wide effect. Operators, monitoring systems, CSI drivers, and ingress controllers all require ClusterRoles to function.
words.longDefinition: Some Kubernetes resources exist outside any namespace: nodes, namespaces, persistentvolumes, clusterroles, storageclasses, and CRDs. These can only be governed by a ClusterRole — a namespace-scoped Role cannot reference them. ClusterRoles follow the same permission structure as Roles (apiGroups, resources, verbs) but operate cluster-wide. A ClusterRoleBinding attaches a ClusterRole to subjects (ServiceAccounts, users, groups) with cluster-wide effect — the subject can act on matching resources in every namespace or on cluster-scoped resources everywhere. A critical pattern: bind a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding (not ClusterRoleBinding) to limit its scope to one namespace — this is how the built-in admin and edit ClusterRoles are used for namespace-level admin access without duplicating Role definitions. The cluster-admin ClusterRole grants every action on every resource and is the Kubernetes superuser equivalent; any subject bound to it can do anything in the cluster. Audit cluster-admin bindings regularly with kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep cluster-admin and keep the list to system components only. Beware of escalation verbs: create on rolebindings or clusterrolebindings gives the subject the ability to grant themselves additional permissions — Kubernetes prevents direct privilege escalation above your current level but indirect paths exist.
words.connector: Think of ClusterRole vs Role like the difference between a master key (ClusterRole) and a floor key (Role) in a multi-storey building: the master key works on every floor and every common area; the floor key only opens rooms on one specific floor.
words.techContext: Our Prometheus server uses a ClusterRole that grants get, list, watch on nodes, pods, and services across all namespaces, bound via a ClusterRoleBinding — the only cluster-wide permission we grant to a non-system service account.
words.exampleSentence: Discovering that our log collector's ClusterRoleBinding referenced cluster-admin instead of a scoped ClusterRole was the highest-priority RBAC finding in our security audit.

codeExample.code:
# ClusterRole: read nodes and pods across all namespaces
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: metrics-collector
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes", "nodes/metrics", "pods", "namespaces"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["metrics.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["nodes", "pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: metrics-collector-binding
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: prometheus
    namespace: monitoring
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: metrics-collector
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

words.etymology: Cluster from Latin clustrum ('a bolt, bar'); Role from Old French role ('list, register'); ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding as Kubernetes API types were introduced with RBAC GA in Kubernetes 1.8 (2017).

words.shortDefinition: API server policy that records every request (who, what, when) to a log sink for compliance and incident investigation.
words.simpleDefinition: Kubernetes Audit Logging records every request made to the API server — who made it (user or ServiceAccount), what action was performed, on which resource, and when — according to a policy that specifies which requests to log at which level of detail. Audit logs are the primary forensic tool after a security incident and the foundation of compliance evidence for SOC 2, PCI DSS, and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark.
words.longDefinition: The Kubernetes API server supports an audit policy that controls which requests are logged and how much detail is captured. An audit policy is a YAML file specifying rules in order; the first matching rule applies. Each rule selects API groups, resources, verbs, users, and namespaces, and assigns one of four logging levels: None (do not log), Metadata (log request metadata — user, verb, resource, timestamp — but not body), Request (log metadata plus request body), and RequestResponse (log metadata plus request and response bodies — useful for debugging but verbose). Audit events are written to a log backend: a JSON file on the API server host (configurable via --audit-log-path) or a webhook backend that forwards events to an aggregation system. The audit log captures the full picture of cluster activity: kubectl exec into pods, Secret reads, privilege escalations, and admission webhook calls. Critical events to audit at RequestResponse level: Secret reads and writes, ServiceAccount token creation, ClusterRoleBinding mutations. Key fields in each audit event: user.username, user.groups, verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.name, objectRef.namespace, sourceIPs, requestReceivedTimestamp. When responding to a security incident, audit logs answer: 'What did the attacker read? What did they create? Which ServiceAccount token did they use?'
words.connector: Think of Kubernetes Audit Logging like a security camera system for the API server: it records every door that opens (every API call), who opened it, and when — without the camera, you have no evidence of what happened after an intrusion.
words.techContext: After our incident, the audit logs let us reconstruct exactly which ServiceAccount was used, which Secrets it read, and which pods it exec'd into — the investigation would have been impossible without them.
words.exampleSentence: The audit log showed that the compromised CI token had listed all Secrets in the production namespace at 03:17 UTC — two hours before the attacker's payload executed.

codeExample.code:
# Audit policy (passed to API server via --audit-policy-file)
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
  # Log Secret reads and writes at RequestResponse level
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets"]

  # Log RBAC mutations at RequestResponse level
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
        resources: ["clusterrolebindings", "rolebindings"]

  # Log all other requests at Metadata level (no body)
  - level: Metadata
    omitStages: [RequestReceived]

words.etymology: Audit from Latin audire ('to hear') — originally referred to an official examination of accounts read aloud; logging from Old Norse logg ('a felled tree', later a ship's log) — adopted into computing for event recording.

words.shortDefinition: KMS-backed encryption at rest for etcd data, ensuring Secrets are not stored in plaintext on the control-plane disk.
words.simpleDefinition: By default, Kubernetes Secrets are stored in etcd with only base64 encoding — readable by anyone with etcd access. Enabling encryption at rest means the API server encrypts Secret data before writing to etcd and decrypts it on read. With a KMS provider, the encryption key lives outside the cluster — in AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault — so even a stolen etcd backup is unreadable without KMS access.
words.longDefinition: A default Kubernetes installation stores Secrets in etcd with base64 encoding — not encryption. Anyone with direct etcd access (through a snapshot, a backup, or an etcd client) can read all Secret values including database passwords, API tokens, and TLS private keys. Kubernetes supports encryption at rest via an EncryptionConfiguration resource on the API server. The provider list determines where encryption keys live: aescbc/aesgcm encrypt with a symmetric key stored in the EncryptionConfiguration file on the control plane — better than plaintext but the key is still on-host. The KMS v2 provider (stable in Kubernetes 1.29) uses envelope encryption: each Secret is encrypted with a per-object data encryption key (DEK) using AES-GCM; the DEK is itself wrapped by a key-encryption key (KEK) that lives in the external KMS and never leaves it. Even a complete etcd dump is unreadable without access to the external KMS. Cloud provider implementations: AWS EKS enables envelope encryption natively via the cluster config using the aws-encryption-provider sidecar. GKE Application-layer secrets encryption is a cluster feature flag. AKS uses the Azure KMS plugin calling Azure Key Vault. After enabling encryption, existing Secrets must be re-encrypted: kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -. The identity provider (no encryption) must remain as a fallback until all objects are migrated.
words.connector: Think of encrypted etcd like a bank vault inside a safety deposit box: etcd is the vault (physically secure), but its contents are further locked in a box whose key (the KEK) is held by the bank (external KMS). Breaking into the vault without the key yields only locked boxes.
words.techContext: After enabling KMS v2 encryption on our EKS cluster, a stolen etcd backup from our disaster-recovery tests showed only ciphertext — confirmed that credentials are protected even if backup storage is compromised.
words.exampleSentence: An etcd encryption audit found that our 18-month-old cluster had stored Secrets in plaintext all along because the encryption provider had never been configured after initial setup.

codeExample.code:
# /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml (passed to kube-apiserver)
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
      - configmaps   # optional: encrypt ConfigMaps too
    providers:
      - kms:
          apiVersion: v2          # KMS v2: per-object DEKs, cached in-memory
          name: aws-kms
          endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
          cachesize: 1000
          timeout: 3s
      - identity: {}              # fallback for reading pre-encryption Secrets

# After enabling, re-encrypt existing Secrets:
# kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

words.etymology: Encrypted from Late Latin encryptare ('to hide in a crypt'); etcd from Unix /etc (configuration directory) + 'd' (distributed) — named by CoreOS circa 2013.

words.shortDefinition: Topology where workloads span multiple independent Kubernetes clusters for geographic distribution or blast-radius reduction.
words.simpleDefinition: Multi-cluster federation describes running workloads across multiple independent Kubernetes clusters, each with its own control plane. Clusters may span geographic regions for low latency, separate environments for blast-radius isolation, or divide tenants for regulatory compliance. GitOps tooling — each cluster running its own ArgoCD or Flux agent — has replaced the failed KubeFed centralised control-plane approach.
words.longDefinition: A single Kubernetes cluster is a single failure domain, a single blast radius, and a single regulatory boundary. Multiple clusters trade operational complexity for isolation. The four forces that push organisations toward multiple clusters: blast-radius isolation (a rogue DaemonSet, broken webhook, or etcd corruption affects all workloads in a single cluster), geographic distribution (latency-sensitive workloads need clusters near their users; active-active multi-region requires independent clusters because a single cluster spanning regions cannot survive a network partition without split-brain), regulatory and data-sovereignty requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, and financial regulations often require data to remain within specific legal jurisdictions), and tenancy isolation (large enterprises find namespace-per-team sharing increasingly fragile). The Kubernetes Federation project (KubeFed) was archived in 2023 after limited adoption — its centralised API approach proved too complex and too fragile. The winning pattern is GitOps: each cluster self-reconciles from Git independently. ArgoCD's ApplicationSet controller fans out Applications to registered clusters; Flux manages clusters by pointing each cluster's Flux agent at the appropriate Git path. Cross-cluster service discovery uses the MCS API (ServiceExport/ServiceImport) implemented by Submariner or cloud-native solutions like GKE Multi-Cluster Services.
words.connector: Think of multi-cluster federation like a franchise restaurant chain: each location (cluster) runs independently with its own kitchen (control plane), but they share the same menu (GitOps config repo) and brand standards (policies). No single location's failure takes down the whole chain.
words.techContext: We run three production clusters — us-east, eu-west, and ap-southeast — each with its own ArgoCD ApplicationSet, sharing a single fleet Git repo; a regional cluster outage affects only its traffic portion.
words.exampleSentence: Multi-cluster federation let us pass the GDPR audit confidently because EU customer data provably never leaves the eu-west cluster, which has independent etcd storage and no cross-cluster volume mounts.

codeExample.code:
# ArgoCD ApplicationSet: deploy the same app to all production clusters
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: my-service
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            tier: production
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "my-service-{{name}}"
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/fleet
        path: apps/my-service
        targetRevision: main
        helm:
          valueFiles:
            - values.yaml
            - "values-{{metadata.labels.region}}.yaml"
      destination:
        server: "{{server}}"
        namespace: my-service
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true

words.etymology: Federation from Latin foedus ('treaty, league') — the political metaphor for independent states cooperating while retaining sovereignty; applied to Kubernetes clusters by the core project circa 2015.

words.shortDefinition: GitOps workflow where promoting a config change to staging or production is done via a reviewed Pull Request merge.
words.simpleDefinition: GitOps environment promotion makes deploying to a new environment a Git operation, not a CLI command. A CI pipeline builds an image and opens a PR in the config repo that bumps the image tag in the target environment's values file. A human reviews and merges the PR; the GitOps controller detects the commit and applies the change. Git history is the deployment record.
words.longDefinition: GitOps environment promotion separates the application source repository (code and Dockerfile) from the environment configuration repository (Kustomize overlays or Helm values files per environment). The promotion flow: CI builds and pushes my-service:abc1234 and opens a PR against the config repo that sets image.tag: abc1234 in clusters/dev/values.yaml. The dev PR is auto-merged; the GitOps controller deploys to dev within minutes. After dev tests pass, a separate PR is opened (manually or by automation) targeting clusters/staging/values.yaml with the same tag. After staging sign-off, a production PR is opened targeting clusters/prod/values.yaml — this PR requires a named approver. Merging it is the production deployment. The Git PR is the deployment record: who approved it, what changed, what CI checks ran on the PR — all of this is in the Git log, satisfying SOC 2, ISO 27001, and most financial regulatory change management requirements. Flux provides an ImageUpdateAutomation controller that automates step 1: it watches an OCI registry, detects a new tag matching a semver policy, and commits the bumped tag to Git. ArgoCD relies on external tooling (Argo CD Image Updater, or a CI step) for the same purpose.
words.connector: Think of environment promotion via Git PR like a formal promotion committee at a company: the candidate (new image) moves through probationary stages (dev, staging), each stage requires sign-off, and the final promotion to a senior role (production) requires a documented approval that is permanently on record.
words.techContext: Our promotion pipeline opens the prod PR automatically after staging smoke tests pass; the tech lead's PR approval is both the human gate and the compliance record for every production deployment.
words.exampleSentence: Environment promotion via Git PR meant that when auditors asked for evidence of who approved the March 15 production change, we simply linked to the GitHub PR — author, reviewer, CI checks, and merge timestamp all in one place.

codeExample.code:
# CI step: bump image tag in dev config repo and open PR
NEW_TAG=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

# Clone config repo
git clone https://github.com/my-org/fleet-config /tmp/fleet
cd /tmp/fleet

# Update dev values file
sed -i "s|image.tag:.*|image.tag: ${NEW_TAG}|" \
  clusters/dev/apps/my-service/values.yaml

git commit -am "chore(dev): bump my-service to ${NEW_TAG}"
git push origin HEAD:bump-my-service-dev-${NEW_TAG}

# Open PR via GitHub CLI
gh pr create \
  --title "deploy: my-service ${NEW_TAG} to dev" \
  --body "Auto-generated by CI. Merge to trigger GitOps deploy."

# For production: same flow but requires --reviewer tech-lead

words.etymology: Environment from Latin environer ('to surround'); promotion from Latin promotio ('a moving forward'); Pull Request is a GitHub-coined term from 2008 for requesting that a branch be pulled and merged.

words.shortDefinition: API server extension that delegates Secret encryption/decryption to an external KMS (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault).
words.simpleDefinition: A KMS Plugin is a sidecar process running alongside the Kubernetes API server that bridges the API server's encryption provider interface to an external key management system. The API server sends DEK wrap/unwrap calls to the plugin over a Unix socket; the plugin calls AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or HashiCorp Vault. The key-encryption key (KEK) never leaves the external KMS.
words.longDefinition: Kubernetes's KMS provider interface (KMS v1 introduced in 1.10; KMS v2 stable in 1.29) allows the API server to delegate Secret encryption to an external key management system. The architecture uses envelope encryption: the API server generates a unique data encryption key (DEK) per Secret, encrypts the Secret data with AES-GCM using the DEK, then sends the DEK to the KMS plugin for wrapping (encryption with the key-encryption key, KEK). The KMS plugin calls the external KMS — AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault — which wraps the DEK and returns the ciphertext DEK. Both the encrypted Secret and the ciphertext DEK are stored in etcd. On read, the API server sends the ciphertext DEK to the plugin for unwrapping; the plugin calls the KMS to recover the DEK; the API server decrypts the Secret. The KEK never leaves the external KMS. KMS v2 improves on v1 by caching DEKs in memory — reducing KMS API call volume dramatically compared to v1 which called the KMS on every read. The KMS plugin must be highly available; if it becomes unreachable, the API server cannot decrypt Secrets and workloads that reference them will fail to start. Cloud-managed Kubernetes services (EKS, GKE, AKS) provide native KMS integration without running a plugin sidecar manually.
words.connector: Think of a KMS Plugin like a bank safety-deposit box attendant: you bring your document (DEK) to the attendant, who locks it in a vault (external KMS) that only the bank controls. When you need the document back, the attendant retrieves it — you never hold the vault key yourself.
words.techContext: Our KMS Plugin connects to AWS KMS via a CMK ARN; the plugin is deployed as a DaemonSet on control-plane nodes with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable: 1 to ensure it survives node drains.
words.exampleSentence: After the KMS Plugin was misconfigured and became unreachable, new pods started failing with SecretNotFound errors because the API server could not decrypt the Secrets needed to inject environment variables.

codeExample.code:
# KMS plugin sidecar in the kube-apiserver static pod (simplified)
# The plugin listens on a Unix socket; the API server connects to it

# EncryptionConfiguration referencing the KMS plugin:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources: [secrets]
    providers:
      - kms:
          apiVersion: v2
          name: aws-kms-us-east-1
          endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
          cachesize: 1000   # cache decrypted DEKs; reduces KMS API calls
          timeout: 3s
      - identity: {}  # fallback for reading pre-encryption secrets

# The aws-encryption-provider sidecar container runs alongside kube-apiserver
# mounting the same socket path

words.etymology: KMS (Key Management Service/System) — generic industry term; plugin from 'plug in' (a connector that extends a system); the Kubernetes KMS provider interface was introduced in Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal KEP-1867.

words.shortDefinition: Single volume mount that aggregates multiple sources (Secrets, ConfigMaps, ServiceAccount token, downward API) into one directory.
words.simpleDefinition: A Projected Volume combines multiple volume sources — Secrets, ConfigMaps, a ServiceAccount token, and downward API values — into a single directory mount inside a container. Instead of mounting four separate volumes into four directories, one projected volume delivers all sources under one path with controlled file permissions and token expiry.
words.longDefinition: Kubernetes supports four volume sources that can be projected: Secret (provides secret data as files), ConfigMap (provides configuration data as files), ServiceAccountToken (provides a bound, audience-scoped, time-limited token — replacing the older auto-mounted legacy token), and DownwardAPI (provides pod metadata — namespace, labels, annotations, resource limits — as files or environment variables). A Projected Volume aggregates these sources into a single filesystem mount point with a configurable defaultMode (file permission bits) applied uniformly. The most important use is the ServiceAccountToken projection: unlike the legacy auto-mounted Secret-based token, a projected ServiceAccountToken has configurable audience (bound to a specific API server or cloud service), expirationSeconds (default 3600 s, minimum 600 s, kubelet rotates automatically before expiry), and path (where inside the projected directory to place the token file). This is the mechanism behind Workload Identity — the IRSA, GKE Workload Identity, and Azure Workload Identity tokens are all projected tokens with cloud-specific audiences. The projected volume can also enforce that all sources are mapped into the same directory with consistent permissions, avoiding the per-source directory proliferation that occurs when mounting multiple volumes separately.
words.connector: Think of a Projected Volume like a single company badge that contains your photo ID, your access card, your business cards, and your car park pass — all encoded on one card instead of four separate items you have to carry.
words.techContext: We use a projected volume to co-locate the ServiceAccountToken (for Workload Identity), the CA bundle ConfigMap, and the application config Secret all under /var/secrets — one mount, clean filesystem layout.
words.exampleSentence: Switching to a projected ServiceAccountToken with expirationSeconds: 3600 replaced the old legacy token Secret that had been permanently mounted in the pod with no expiry — a security improvement with no application code change.

codeExample.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-projected-volume
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-org/app:1.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: secrets-and-config
          mountPath: /var/secrets
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: secrets-and-config
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0444   # read-only for all sources
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
              expirationSeconds: 3600
              audience: sts.amazonaws.com   # AWS IRSA audience
          - configMap:
              name: app-config
              items:
                - key: app.properties
                  path: app.properties
          - secret:
              name: tls-certs
              items:
                - key: tls.crt
                  path: tls.crt
          - downwardAPI:
              items:
                - path: namespace
                  fieldRef:
                    fieldPath: metadata.namespace

words.etymology: Projected from Latin proiectus ('thrown forward') — in the sense of mapping or consolidating information into a single representation; the Projected Volume type was introduced in Kubernetes 1.11 (2018).
